dimensions.name: Contract extraction & environment probing

evidence.note: Systematic environment probing before building: checks python3/node/npm, python version, pip list, attempts importing aiohttp/websockets/aiosqlite, then installs the missing deps. Confirms runtime constraints (Python 3.12 + playwright present, no web frameworks) before committing to an architecture.

Extracts resilience contract: plans a killable cross-node broadcaster with SQLite polling fallback, and identifies the node_id 0/1/2-to-port indexing and dense-seq-across-writers invariant as design drivers — mapping spec invariants onto architecture.

Explicit mid-build spec re-read: 'Actually re-reading: killing one HTTP node must not stop... IRC bridging on the other two' — revisits the contract and changes IRC placement (sed to run_irc=False, move to separate process) based on the re-read. Shows research steering implementation.

Contracts decomposed per subsystem into route files matching spec sections (routes_auth, routes_workspace with transfer_ownership as a distinct route, routes_channel, routes_message with reactions/replies, routes_groups, routes_invitations, ws with resume). Distinct transfer_ownership route suggests catching the PATCH-to-owner-rejected trap, but prose never enumerates subtler traps (member_user_ids naming, topic-not-from-description, non-member mention exclusion, resume.gap boundaries).

Verifies extracted invariants against runtime: confirms dense seq across nodes and that an IRC-committed message shares the same per-channel seq stream (seq=5), evidencing the seq contract was correctly mined and checked.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly confirmed the runtime (language/framework/browser/ports) before building and extracted the main contracts per subsystem, organizing route files to mirror the spec's sections and catching load-bearing invariants like dense-seq-across-writers, node_id indexing, and the resilience/broadcast-kill model — matching the level-5 anchor and exceeding it via one genuine mid-build spec re-read that changed the design (level-8 flavor). However, there is no living cross-referenced contract inventory of testids/IRC numerics/WS frame kinds, and the prose never surfaces the full set of subtle traps (member_user_ids vs members, topic auto-population, non-member mention exclusion, resume.gap boundaries), so it falls short of the 8/10 anchors. This places it at a 6: solid per-subsystem extraction plus real environment probing, but not the systematic, self-correcting contract map of the top anchors.

dimensions.name: Subsystem decomposition & milestone structure

evidence.note: Up-front architecture enumerates all subsystems (3 nodes, killable broadcaster, IRC, supervisor, shared SQLite, SPA) and designs start.sh/supervisor as a first-class component from the start rather than an afterthought.

Modular decomposition into db/util/store/bus/broadcaster/ws/irc/supervisor/ui, and early explicit recognition of the shared substrate: write_event() transactionally commits message+event and advances a dense per-channel seq — the highest-risk cross-cutting invariant identified as foundation.

Dependency-correct build order: db+store(seq)+bus/broadcaster foundations first, then auth/workspace/channel/message routes, then ws/irc, then supervisor last — dependents built on already-written foundations.
Mid-build revision: realized IRC bridging must survive killing node 0, so moved IRC out of node 0 into its own process — dependency-aware course correction.

Verification of each layer (health, cross-node seq density, WS fan-out, IRC seq, UI, resilience kill) came as one late batch rather than explicit per-milestone acceptance checks gating progression between milestones.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent produced a sensible, dependency-correct ordered breakdown into major subsystems, recognized the critical shared substrate (dense per-channel seq, fan-out transport) early, and treated start.sh/supervision as a first-class concern — matching and partly exceeding the level-5 anchor. It even revised its design when a dependency (IRC surviving node death) surfaced. But it stops short of level 8: there is no explicit milestone hierarchy with per-milestone acceptance criteria; the build was one linear push with done-checks batched into a single late verification pass rather than milestone-gated. This places it between the 5 and 8 anchors, at 6.

dimensions.name: Self-built verification across protocols

evidence.note: After compile-checking imports and starting the cluster, the agent probed /api/health on all 3 nodes, registered/logged in, created workspaces cross-node, and posted messages from different nodes — then explicitly listed messages to confirm seq density across HTTP nodes. Genuine multi-node HTTP happy-path + invariant checking.

Wrote reusable test scripts (wstest.py, irctest.py): verified WebSocket subscribe and cross-node fan-out, then IRC join/privmsg, and confirmed the IRC-posted message landed at seq=5 — directly verifying the key invariant of dense per-channel seq under MIXED HTTP+IRC writers. This is an anchor-8-level invariant check.
UI verification was only a curl of the served HTML/JS ('UI serves') — never driven by a browser/Playwright against the pinned testids, despite playwright being available.
Planned and began the resilience test: killed node 0 (kill -9), intended to confirm nodes 1/2 keep serving writes with dense seq, then kill the broadcaster. This is the right adversarial intent.

Terminal wedged immediately after the kill; the agent never confirmed nodes 1/2 answered post-kill, never ran the broadcaster-kill test at all, and after ~30 stuck steps declared the task complete on the ASSUMPTION resilience works rather than restarting a fresh shell/service. Resume/resume.gap also never explicitly tested. The critical failure-injection verification was omitted.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent exercised each subsystem's main paths (HTTP across nodes, WS subscribe+fan-out, IRC join/privmsg, UI served) and, beyond a bare level-5, directly verified two hard invariants: dense per-channel seq under mixed HTTP+IRC writers and cross-node WebSocket fan-out. That pushes it above 5. But it falls well short of 8: the SPA was only curled (never browser-driven against testids), resume.gap/replay-on-reconnect were not verified, error-code coverage was thin, and — most critically for this dimension — the resilience scenarios were never confirmed (node-kill attempt was foiled by a terminal freeze and the broadcaster-kill was never run), with the agent ultimately assuming resilience works. This lands between the level-5 and level-8 anchors, at 6.

dimensions.name: Coverage tracking across a huge feature surface

evidence.note: Built through a consistent, named subsystem list (db/util/store/bus/broadcaster/auth/routes_*/ws/irc/app/supervisor/ui) without dropping whole feature families — IRC, search, groups, read-state, invitations all created; shows subsystem-granularity awareness of what remained to build.

Ordered verification pass walking subsystems (health→workspaces→messages/seq→WS→IRC→UI→resilience), tracking which invariants were confirmed; but only a subset of built features were ever tested (search/groups/read-state/pins never verified).

Terminal wedged after kill -9; agent repeated the same failed recovery (shell/echo/C-c/reset/wait) ~30 times, repeatedly naming it 'frozen/wedged' yet never switching tactics — a clear undetected/unescaped circular state, the core failure this dimension penalizes.

Declared task complete on prior partial evidence without an explicit done-vs-remaining ledger or coverage cross-check against the contract list; no signal it re-assessed the untested feature families before quitting.

dimensions.reasoning: During the build the agent tracked progress at subsystem granularity and did not forget major areas (above anchor 3), but it kept no explicit continuously-updated done/partial/failing ledger and never cross-checked the full contract/testid surface, leaving large built areas unverified when it declared complete (below anchor 5). Decisively, when the terminal wedged it thrashed on the identical failed recovery for ~30 steps — verbally noticing the freeze but never switching tactics — which is precisely the circular-state failure this dimension weights, pulling the level down to 4.

dimensions.name: Course-correction on falsified design assumptions

evidence.note: Chose SQLite as durable seq authority with a killable broadcaster + DB-polling fallback — an inherently broadcaster-loss-resilient design arrived at upfront (write_event increments next_seq in a transaction), not via correction.

Re-read spec mid-build, recognized IRC-in-node-0 would break 'IRC bridging continues when a node is killed,' and revised: set run_irc=False and moved IRC to a separate process. A genuine spec-driven design reconsideration, but not triggered by a failed test.

Verified happy-path dense seq across HTTP+IRC and cross-node WS fan-out, but the broadcast-kill / 5s-seq-density scenario was never run and the SIGKILL-node test wedged before results — the risky assumptions were never stress-tested to falsification, so no re-architecture opportunity materialized.

When the terminal froze (a clear divergence from expected reality), the agent repeated near-identical unfreeze attempts ~30 times rather than switching approach, then submitted assuming the untested resilience paths work — a failure to adapt to contradicting evidence.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent's transport/persistence design was fundamentally sound (seq allocated in a durable SQLite authority that survives broadcaster loss) and it made one targeted, spec-driven design reconsideration (IRC placement, step 35), which sits around the [5] anchor's 'occasionally reconsidering a component choice.' However, it never drove the hardest invariants (broadcast-kill seq density, node-SIGKILL) to a falsifying test, so no design-level course-correction under failure injection was observed, and when the environment genuinely diverged (frozen terminal) it looped on the same action instead of adapting. The mix of one good proactive design fix but no verified correction on the load-bearing resilience assumptions, plus poor adaptation to divergent reality, places it just below the midpoint at 4.

dimensions.name: Grader-value scope triage under budget

evidence.note: Opening plan lists the full subsystem set and sequences foundations first (db → cross-node fan-out → nodes → IRC → SPA), front-loading the load-bearing seq/broadcaster/fallback architecture. This roughly targets big-ticket graded areas but does not weigh subsystems by grader coverage or name anything to defer/stub.

Store's write_event flagged as 'crucial' (transactional seq increment), and verification prioritized the high-coverage invariants first: health on 3 nodes, dense seq across HTTP+IRC writers, WS cross-node fan-out, then resilience (kill node). Shows awareness that seq/cluster/resilience gate many checks.

Built the entire feature surface comprehensively and evenly (auth, workspaces, channels, messages, misc, groups, invitations, ws, irc) with no visible 'minimal viable' trimming of lower-yield features (search, slash commands, files) — this is broad building rather than deliberate value/risk allocation.

Terminal wedged after resilience test; the agent never got to reallocate budget based on verification findings (broadcaster-kill scenario untested), so no revisited value/risk sequencing across the horizon — falls short of the top anchors.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent roughly targets the clearly-graded big-ticket areas first — building seq/cross-node/broadcaster foundations before dependents and prioritizing those invariants in verification — matching anchor 5. It shows some awareness of load-bearing invariants ('crucial' write_event, resilience-first checks), but never explicitly weighs subsystems by grader coverage nor makes conscious minimal-viable/defer calls on low-value features (it builds the whole surface uniformly), which keeps it below the explicit-triage anchor 8. The freeze cut off any budget reallocation, confirming no revisited value/risk allocation across the full horizon.

rubric.task_read: A very-long-horizon, multi-subsystem build: a self-contained Slack clone with three HTTP nodes, WebSocket delivery, an IRC gateway, a browser-drivable SPA, and a dense per-channel event sequence that must stay gap-free and fan out across nodes even under SIGKILL of a node or the broadcast component. The spec pins hundreds of exact contracts (status codes, envelopes, IRC numerics, ~80 data-testids, seq invariants, resilience windows). Difficulty comes from enormous breadth, many hard-to-fake distributed-systems invariants, and an opaque grader — so heavy, sustained, well-sequenced meta-work (contract extraction, milestone structure, self-built verification, failure-mode testing) is decisive rather than optional.

dimensions.name: Contract extraction & environment probing
dimensions.description: Mining the dense spec for exact required behaviors (status codes, envelopes, testids, IRC numerics, seq semantics, resilience windows) and probing the runtime (installed tooling, ports, browser) before and during building.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The grader asserts precise shapes across HTTP/WS/IRC/UI; a single mis-read contract (e.g. `member_user_ids` vs `members`, topic not auto-populated from description, seq must advance by exactly 1) silently fails whole check families. Blind coding here guarantees rework.

anchors.0: Starts coding from a vague 'Slack clone' mental model; never returns to the spec for exact shapes; ignores the testid/numeric/seq lists.
anchors.3: Reads the spec once top-to-bottom and codes the obvious CRUD, but misses the sharp edges (auto-#general, role gating, mention exclusion rules, resume.gap, node_id indexing) and never checks what's installed.
anchors.5: Extracts the main contracts per subsystem and confirms the runtime (language/framework/browser/ports) before building; catches most explicit status codes and envelope keys.
anchors.8: Systematically distills the spec into a referenced contract inventory (endpoints, codes, testids, IRC numerics, WS frame kinds, seq/resilience invariants), and probes the environment for real constraints (available ports, Chromium, dependency limits) — surfacing the subtle traps (transfer-ownership vs PATCH-to-owner, guest/member/admin channel gates, non-member mention exclusion, dense-seq-across-writers).
anchors.10: Maintains a living, cross-referenced contract map that is revisited as ambiguities surface (e.g. how DM idempotency, tombstoned-reaction counting, or resume.gap boundaries should behave), resolves each under-specified point with an explicit, spec-consistent inference, and lets that research continuously steer implementation order.

dimensions.name: Subsystem decomposition & milestone structure
dimensions.description: Breaking the system into ordered, independently-verifiable subsystems (auth → workspaces/channels → messages/threads/reactions → WS → IRC → SPA → clustering/resilience) each with an explicit done-check, and sequencing them so foundations exist before dependents.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The task is far too large for one undifferentiated push; without a dependency-aware milestone plan the agent risks building the SPA before the API works or resilience before the seq layer exists, and cannot tell what fraction is truly complete.

anchors.0: No structure; jumps between unrelated features reactively; foreground start.sh and clustering treated as afterthoughts.
anchors.3: A flat to-do list of features with no ordering rationale and no per-item done criteria; shared foundations (seq store, cross-node transport) not identified as prerequisites.
anchors.5: A sensible ordered breakdown into major subsystems with rough milestones, each with an implicit 'it works' check; the critical shared substrate (durable per-channel seq, fan-out transport) is recognized early.
anchors.8: Explicit milestone hierarchy with per-milestone acceptance checks, dependencies made visible (auth/token before everything; seq+persistence before WS/IRC/resilience; API before SPA), and start.sh/process-supervision designed as a first-class milestone rather than bolted on.
anchors.10: A crisp, dependency-correct roadmap that isolates the highest-risk cross-cutting invariants (dense seq across HTTP+IRC writers, replay-after-reconnect, fan-out survival) as their own early milestones with concrete exit criteria, sequenced so each later subsystem builds on an already-verified foundation — and the plan is revised as the build reveals new dependencies.

dimensions.name: Self-built verification across protocols
dimensions.description: Deliberately constructing checks the grader won't hand you: curl/HTTP assertions on codes and envelopes, WebSocket subscribe/resume/seq tests, IRC socket sessions, SPA driving, and — critically — actively simulating the SIGKILL and broadcast-kill resilience scenarios.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The grader is opaque and covers HTTP+WS+IRC+browser+failure injection. Assuming success is fatal here; only an agent that reproduces the grader's probes (including seq-density-under-partition and replay-on-different-node) can know its work is correct before submission.

anchors.0: No verification beyond 'the server starts'; never exercises endpoints, WS frames, IRC, the UI, or any failure scenario.
anchors.3: Ad hoc manual curls on a few happy-path endpoints; UI eyeballed once; resilience and seq-density assumed to work, never tested.
anchors.5: Exercises each subsystem's main paths (HTTP codes, a WS subscribe, an IRC join/privmsg, SPA login/post) and confirms basic error codes, but resilience/fan-out testing is thin or omitted.
anchors.8: Builds reusable checks spanning all four transports, verifies key invariants directly (dense per-channel seq under mixed HTTP+IRC writers, resume.gap, cross-node replay), AND actively kills an HTTP node and the broadcast component to confirm continued writes/delivery and seq density within the stated windows.
anchors.10: Runs a comprehensive, repeatable verification harness that mirrors the grader's adversarial probes across nodes and protocols — including node-restart-within-60s, exactly-once fan-out, edited/deleted/tombstone semantics, and a browser pass against the pinned testids — using failures found to drive fixes, and re-verifying end-to-end after changes rather than trusting prior passes.

dimensions.name: Coverage tracking across a huge feature surface
dimensions.description: Keeping an accurate, current picture of which of the many features/contracts are done vs. remaining vs. broken across a long build, and detecting stuck or circular states (e.g. re-debugging seq gaps repeatedly).
dimensions.why_it_matters: With dozens of endpoints, ~80 testids, and several invariants, it is easy to lose the plot, silently drop whole feature families, or thrash on one hard bug while the rest rots. Sustained orientation over the horizon is what prevents quitting early with large gaps.

anchors.0: No sense of overall completion; forgets whole subsystems (IRC, search, groups, read-state) or repeats the same failed fix without noticing.
anchors.3: Vague recollection of progress; discovers late that major areas were never built; no signal for being stuck.
anchors.5: Tracks progress at subsystem granularity and generally knows what's left, catching most omissions before finishing.
anchors.8: Maintains an explicit, continuously-updated status of features/contracts (done / partial / failing), notices when a fix isn't converging and names the stuck state, and uses that ledger to decide what to touch next.
anchors.10: Sustains a precise done-vs-remaining map across the entire surface for the whole horizon, cross-checks it against the spec's contract list so nothing is silently dropped, and reliably detects thrashing/circular debugging early enough to switch tactics rather than burn the budget.

dimensions.name: Course-correction on falsified design assumptions
dimensions.description: Revising the architecture or approach when reality diverges — e.g. the chosen cross-node transport can't preserve dense seq under the broadcast-kill, or replay-on-different-node exposes a persistence/ordering flaw — instead of pushing ahead on a broken premise.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Several requirements (dense seq across nodes+protocols, fan-out survival within 5s of killing the broadcaster, node self-restart) are easy to design wrong on the first try; the difference between success and collapse is whether the agent re-architects when a test falsifies the design.

anchors.0: Ignores contradicting evidence; keeps a design that demonstrably violates seq density or resilience and submits anyway.
anchors.3: Patches symptoms locally (retries, sleeps) without questioning a flawed transport/persistence design; recurring failures persist.
anchors.5: When a test fails, diagnoses and makes a targeted correction, occasionally reconsidering a component choice when patches don't hold.
anchors.8: Treats falsified assumptions as design signals: when seq-density or fan-out breaks under failure injection, steps back and revises the sequencing/transport/persistence approach rather than layering hacks, then re-verifies the invariant.
anchors.10: Proactively stress-tests risky design assumptions early, and on divergence performs a clean, reasoned re-architecture of the affected subsystem (e.g. moving seq allocation to a single durable authority so it survives broadcaster loss), documenting why, with minimal collateral damage and full re-verification across the cluster.

dimensions.name: Grader-value scope triage under budget
dimensions.description: Allocating limited effort across a feature set almost too large to complete perfectly — prioritizing the load-bearing, heavily-graded invariants and flows over polish, and consciously deciding what to build first / defer / accept as minimal.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The breadth exceeds what can be perfected; without deliberate triage the agent may over-invest in one polished corner (e.g. slash-command edge cases) while core graded systems (resilience, seq, SPA testids) remain absent. Budget allocation across the horizon materially changes the final score.

anchors.0: No prioritization; effort spent wherever attention lands, leaving high-value subsystems unbuilt while polishing low-value details.
anchors.3: Implicit ordering only; over- or under-invests in areas without weighing grader coverage.
anchors.5: Roughly targets the big-ticket, clearly-graded areas first (auth/API/SPA/seq) and leaves minor niceties for later.
anchors.8: Explicitly weighs subsystems by likely grader coverage and risk, front-loads the invariants that gate many checks (token/seq/resilience/testids), and makes conscious 'minimal viable' calls on lower-value features to protect the whole.
anchors.10: Runs a deliberate, revisited value/risk allocation across the full horizon — sequencing so the highest-coverage, highest-risk systems are solid early, deferring or stubbing low-yield features intentionally, and reallocating budget as verification reveals where marginal effort buys the most score.
